title: Redwood rate limits & org/project keys demo with UrbanMed Health

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Jared Lopez (Redwood SE), Dr. Ananya Rao (CTO, UrbanMed), Mike Chen (Eng Manager), Priya Singh (Security), Luis Alvarez (DevOps)
---
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um hi Ananya, Mike, Priya, Luis. We really appreciate you taking the time. I'll hand it to Jared to do a quick walk through of how we handle rate limits, org and project keys, and a quick Console demo.
[00:17] Jared Lopez: Cool thanks Sarah. So quick agenda — org vs project keys, quota model, demo in Console, API examples, and then Q&A. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:31] Dr. Ananya Rao: Great thanks. We're particularly interested in two things: one is multi-tenant isolation — we want to make sure a noisy tenant doesn't affect others — and two is key management and auditing for compliance.
[00:44] Jared Lopez: Totally. So at a high level Redwood supports org-level keys and project-level keys. Org keys are high-privilege and typically used for admin operations, project keys are scoped to a project and its quotas. For UrbanMed you'd probably create a project per customer environment — staging/prod or customer-id.
[01:02] Mike Chen: Quick question — can a single request include a project header and an org header? How does precedence work?
[01:10] Jared Lopez: Good question. The precedence is: if a request includes a project key header it is evaluated against the project's quotas and rate limits; if only an org key is present it falls back to org-level defaults. If both are present we honor the project scope for throttling and billing. There's also route-level overrides.
[01:28] Priya Singh: And by header you mean the API key in the Authorization header? Do you have an example?
[01:34] Jared Lopez: Yes — Authorization: Bearer <project_key>. We also support X-Redwood-Project-Key for internal routing in some SDKs, older clients might see that. Example cURL I'll paste after.
[01:48] Sarah Kim: Note: some transcripts out there call it 'red wood' keys — it's Redwood keys, definitely.
[01:55] Luis Alvarez: Ok — on quotas, does Redwood do token-based quotas or request-based quotas? We have variable-length responses.
[02:03] Jared Lopez: We support token quotas (monthly/rolling windows) and request/QPS quotas. You can set both. For example you can limit a project to 1M tokens per month and also cap at 100 QPS. Burst behaviour is configurable — we have a bucketed leaky-bucket model so short bursts are allowed up to a burst limit, then you get hard rate limit responses.
[02:30] Dr. Ananya Rao: Is burst token usage charged? Like if they burn tokens in a burst does that count toward their monthly quota?
[02:37] Jared Lopez: Yes bursts still count against token consumption. The burst just controls the instantaneous QPS throttle; tokens are metered as usual.
[02:44] Mike Chen: Can we have per-route limits? We want to cap embeddings to a lower QPS than chat generation.
[02:52] Jared Lopez: Absolutely — route-specific policies are common. You can apply per-model, per-route, or per-endpoint limits in the Console. So you might set embeddings endpoints to 20 QPS and chat generation to 50 QPS under the same project.
[03:06] Priya Singh: From a compliance perspective we need audit logs of key usage and rotation events — retention 1 year. Do you store request-level logs with tokens or redacted?
[03:16] Jared Lopez: We keep request metadata and high-level usage logs. Payloads are redacted for customer-controlled privacy settings. For Private deployments you can enable full request logging into your SIEM if required. We also have KMS integrations for key wrapping and HSM options in Private.
[03:32] Dr. Ananya Rao: You mentioned Private — we'd likely consider Dedicated or Private for PHI workflows. Does the rate limiter behave differently in Dedicated pools?
[03:41] Jared Lopez: No functional difference — the runtime enforces the same quota semantics. The difference is capacity predictability and isolation. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput so you're less likely to hit a noisy neighbor at the infra layer.
[03:54] Sarah Kim: If helpful we can map Dedicated SKUs to your estimated QPS and tokens and show expected tail latency.
[04:02] Mike Chen: That would be helpful.
[04:05] Jared Lopez: Moving to the Console demo — I'll share screen. (pause) Alright, top nav -> Organization -> Rate limits.
[04:20] Jared Lopez: Here you can see projects listed. Selecting a project shows its current usage, monthly token quota, QPS, and burst window. You can toggle enforcement from soft to hard — soft will log and alert but not block, hard will return 429.
[04:39] Dr. Ananya Rao: Soft enforcement is interesting for ramping. Does it generate alerts to Slack or PagerDuty?
[04:46] Jared Lopez: Yes — integrations for Slack, PagerDuty, and webhook. Alerts can include usage thresholds (e.g., 80% of quota) and sustained QPS spikes.
[04:56] Luis Alvarez: Is there an API to read current quota consumption? We'd like to surface this in our internal app.
[05:02] Jared Lopez: Yep — /v1/usage endpoints give granular usage per project and per-route. We'll provide sample SDK calls.
[05:12] Sarah Kim: I'll paste the cURL example in chat after the call: Authorization header examples, and the X-Redwood-Project-Key note.
[05:20] Mike Chen: Regarding key rotation — can keys be rotated without downtime? We have long-lived services.
[05:26] Jared Lopez: Yes — we recommend creating a new key, update your services to the new key, then revoke the old one. The Console supports staged rotation and you can set key expiry. For programmatic rotation we have API endpoints to create and revoke keys.
[05:41] Priya Singh: For audit we need to know who rotated which key and when. Does Redwood log actor identity?
[05:48] Jared Lopez: Yes — audit logs record actor (SSO identity or service account), timestamp, and action. Logs are exportable. For Private deployments you can ship logs to your SIEM for long-term retention.
[06:00] Dr. Ananya Rao: What about rate-limiting in the SDKs — are retries handled? We use exponential backoff in our clients, will Redwood return Retry-After?
[06:10] Jared Lopez: We return 429 with Retry-After headers for rate-limited responses. Our SDKs include retry helpers but we recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter.
[06:20] Sarah Kim: Real quick — customers often ask about model fallbacks if a model is throttled; you can set an automatic fallback policy to route to a cheaper variant. Jared do a quick example?
[06:31] Jared Lopez: Sure — in routing policies you can set a primary model and fallback chain. If the primary is at capacity the request can be routed to a quantized variant or older version. Useful to keep latency SLOs. Keep in mind output quality tradeoffs.
[06:50] Mike Chen: How granular can policies be? Per-customer, per-route, per-model?
[06:55] Jared Lopez: All of the above — you can compose policies. For multi-tenant scenarios we recommend project-per-tenant and then use project-level routing plus org-level defaults.
[07:08] (audio: slight cross talk)
[07:15] Dr. Ananya Rao: Can we programmatically create projects during onboarding? We auto-provision environments for customers.
[07:21] Jared Lopez: Absolutely — the control plane has APIs for project creation, key issuance, and quota assignment. Also org-level templates so you can create a project from a template with default limits.
[07:33] Priya Singh: Any built-in protections for credential exfiltration? E.g., rate limits on key creation or alerts on many failed auth attempts?
[07:41] Jared Lopez: Yes — you can set thresholds on key creation and admin actions, and there's anomalous activity detection alerts. Failed auth attempts are logged and can fire alerts.
[07:53] Luis Alvarez: About cost control — can we set hard token caps that prevent overages? We want a hard guardrail so accidental spikes don't charge us.
[08:01] Jared Lopez: Yes hard caps are supported. If you hit a hard token cap further requests will be rejected until quota refresh. You can also set soft thresholds to notify before hitting cap.
[08:12] Sarah Kim: Quick demo of the API header — (types) here's a cURL sample:

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer proj_abc123" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-open-1","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the clinical note"}] }'

[08:35] Jared Lopez: And for reading usage:

curl -X GET https://api.redwood.ai/v1/usage?project=proj_abc123 -H "Authorization: Bearer org_admin_key"

[08:50] Mike Chen: Ok that helps. Any quirks with streaming responses and rate limits?
[08:56] Jared Lopez: Streaming uses the same token metering; partial streams count tokens as they're produced. For long streaming sessions we recommend per-connection QPS limits to avoid holding resources.
[09:08] Dr. Ananya Rao: What happens to in-flight requests when you revoke a key? Are they killed?
[09:15] Jared Lopez: Currently revocation prevents new requests; in-flight requests continue to completion for stability, but you can enable stricter revocation policies in Private deployments if needed.
[09:28] Priya Singh: Network diagram — do you have a sample of private deployment network flows (VPC peering, egress controls)?
[09:35] Sarah Kim: Yes we'll share the network diagram PDF and the Private/Dedicated deployment guide.
[09:40] Luis Alvarez: For POC we'd like a small Dedicated pool to test latency and isolation — what's the typical lead time?
[09:46] Sarah Kim: For Dedicated we typically have a short provisioning lead time — a week or two depending on region and capacity. For Private on-prem it's longer. We'll include expected timelines with the SKU.
[09:58] Jared Lopez: One more note — console shows live token burn rate and a historical chart so you can see spikes and correlate with traces. That ties into our tracing hooks and request IDs.
[10:10] Dr. Ananya Rao: That's useful for debugging.
[10:14] Mike Chen: Any integration for Envoy or gateway-level rate limiting? We want to keep control in our gateway too.
[10:21] Jared Lopez: You can front Redwood with Envoy and use per-route headers or use our API to sync quotas. We have reference configs for Envoy rate-limiter integrations.
[10:32] (short pause)
[10:36] Sarah Kim: Alright let's open questions from the team.
[10:40] Mike Chen: Would you be able to map our traffic profile (we send periodic batched embeddings, occasional large chat) to a recommended batching and quantization config?
[10:49] Jared Lopez: Yes — that's part of Redwood Optimize. We can analyze your prompt set and recommend batching sizes, quant profiles, and which model variants to use for each workload to balance cost/latency. I'll put that as an action item.
[11:04] Priya Singh: Last security question — for SSO we want SCIM provisioning and role-based access. Are those supported?
[11:11] Jared Lopez: Supported — SAML/SSO, SCIM, RBAC with granular roles, and per-key scopes.
[11:18] Dr. Ananya Rao: Ok great. Wrapping up — recap next steps?
[11:22] Sarah Kim: Quick recap: Sarah sends Dedicated SKU pricing and SOC2/network docs; Jared runs a benchmark with your sample prompts; UrbanMed to provide prompts and target QPS; schedule POC scoping on Mar 10.
[11:35] Mike Chen: Sounds good.
[11:37] Dr. Ananya Rao: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[11:40] Sarah Kim: Thanks all. We'll follow up by EOD with the materials.
[11:45] (call ends)
---
Notes: transcript has minor transcription errors (e.g., "kay-vee cache" for KV cache, "red wood" heard once). Shared artifacts: Dedicated SKU spreadsheet (link placeholder), SOC2 summary PDF (link placeholder), network diagram PDF, sample cURL snippets in chat.
